title: Distant opposition
summary: Take the opposition from afar, head on, along the diagonal or along the rank, to reach the key squares or to defend.
part.distant.title: Distant opposition
part.distant.summary: With the kings far apart, take the opposition from afar. With every step of the other king, it turns into direct opposition.
step.t_lesson: The key squares of the g3 pawn are far from both kings. Think: if the white king runs straight for them, does the black king get there first? What is the right first step?
step.t_lesson.hint1: Put the kings on the same file and count the squares between them.
step.t_lesson.hint2: With an odd number of squares between the kings and the other side to move, the opposition is yours.
step.intro: The key squares of the g3-pawn are f5, g5 and h5. If I rush towards them without a plan, the black king arrives first and stands in front. Distant opposition decides the struggle: the kings stand on the same file, with an odd number of intervening squares, one, three or five, and the opponent to move. It works because I can reduce the distance while keeping the opposition until it becomes direct, with just one square between the kings. The Cuban {{Capablanca|jose-raul-capablanca}}, world champion from 1921 to 1927, states the rule from the other side: with an even number of intervening squares, the player to move takes the opposition.
step.d_distant: Watch distant opposition turn into direct opposition, one step at a time.
step.d_distant.m1: 1.Ke4. The black king's file, three squares in between, e5, e6 and e7, and Black to move. The distant opposition is mine.
step.d_distant.m2: The black king cannot pass. He leaves the e-file for the f-file.
step.d_distant.m3: 2.Kf5. I go to the new file and stand in front of him, one square in between. And f5 is already a key square of the g3-pawn.
step.d_distant.m4: He gives way again, now to the g-file.
step.d_distant.m5: 3.Kg5. Face to face again, on another key square. From here the pawn queens.
step.convert: This time the black king will answer differently. Take the distant opposition and, after each of his moves, face him until you reach the key square.
step.convert.hint:
Before advancing the pawn, look for a king square that leaves an odd number of squares between the kings. Then see whether you can shorten the distance or reach a key square.

The refutations are organized by decision. Each variation begins with an attempt that fails to preserve the objective; it is not the recommended line.

Decision 1
The king needs to gain space before the pawn advances.
1.Ke3 Ke7 2.g4 Ke6. The position allows a draw.
1.g4 Kd7 2.g5 Kd6. The position allows a draw.

Decision 2
Here, advancing to the available key square is valid; leaving the struggle or spending the reserve allows a blockade.
2.Kf4 Kf6 3.g4 Kg6. The position allows a draw.
2.g4 Ke6 3.g5 Ke7. The position allows a draw.

Decision 3
The king must reach the key square before releasing the pawn.
3.g4 Kg6 4.g5 Kxg5. The position allows a draw.
step.convert.done:
You preserved the objective. The demonstration illustrates this plan: the king gained space before the pawn advanced. Distant opposition was useful because it allowed a key square to be reached.

The demonstrated line is 1.Ke4 Ke7 2.Ke5 Kf7 3.Kf5. An equivalent alternative may complete the practice before this sequence ends.
Also preserve the objective: 2.Kf5.
part.diagonal.title: Diagonal opposition
part.diagonal.summary: When the file is out of reach, the opposition also works along a diagonal.
step.t_diagonal: The black king guards the key squares of the e3-pawn, and the white king's most natural move looks good, but it may not be. Which square leaves the black king without a good answer?
step.t_diagonal.hint1: The kings need not be on the same file: a diagonal works too, with one square between them.
step.t_diagonal.hint2: After coming in along the diagonal, wherever the black king goes, look to face him again, from any side.
step.diagonal: So far the kings were on the same file. Now they are not, and the bridge is the diagonal. 1.Ke4 looks natural, but after 1...Ke6 it is the black king that has direct opposition, and the e3-pawn does not get through. The way in is 1.Kf4: the diagonal f4, e5, d6, one square in between, and Black to move. From then on I always stand facing him, from above or from the side.
step.d_diagonal: Watch the diagonal turn into direct opposition.
step.d_diagonal.m1: 1.Kf4. Kings on the diagonal f4, e5, d6, one square in between, and Black to move.
step.d_diagonal.m2: The black king goes to e6, in front of the pawn, to block the e-file.
step.d_diagonal.m3: 2.Ke4. Now face to face on the e-file, one square in between: direct opposition, and Black to move.
step.d_diagonal.m4: He has to give way. He goes to d6, from where he still guards d5 and e5.
step.d_diagonal.m5: 3.Kf5. The key square that was left free. With the king here, the e3-pawn queens.
step.diagonalMove: Come in along the diagonal; this time the black king will answer differently.
step.diagonalMove.hint:
First look for diagonal opposition. After the reply, identify the rank or file on which your king can prevent the opposing king from approaching and reach a key square.

The refutations are organized by decision. Each variation begins with an attempt that fails to preserve the objective; it is not the recommended line.

Decision 1
The diagonal entry prepares useful opposition; the pawn advance and direct approach give the defender the time it needs.
1.e4 Ke5 2.Ke2 Kxe4. The position allows a draw.
1.Ke4 Ke6 2.Kd3 Kd5. The position allows a draw.

Decision 2
The key square along the rank is decisive; a pawn check cannot replace the king’s position.
2.e4+ Ke6 3.e5 Kd7. The position allows a draw.
step.diagonalMove.done:
You preserved the objective. The demonstration illustrates this plan: the diagonal prepared opposition along the rank and access to a key square. The form of opposition was chosen for the entry it allows.

The demonstrated line is 1.Kf4 Kd5 2.Kf5. An equivalent alternative may complete the practice before this sequence ends.
part.defend.title: In defence
part.defend.summary: The defender uses the same rule. He takes the opposition from afar, even by stepping back, and follows the attacking king.
step.t_carlsenSo: Now a real game, from the defender's side. {{Stavanger|stavanger}}, 2017, {{Norway Chess|norway-chess}}: {{Magnus Carlsen|magnus-carlsen}}, with White, against {{Wesley So|wesley-so}}. The knights came off on move 53, and So was a pawn down, two white pawns against one. The white king wants to get in and capture the h6-pawn. Only one move draws. Which one?
step.t_carlsenSo.hint1: Count the squares between the kings on the f-file.
step.t_carlsenSo.hint2: Two squares in between is an even number: on the move, you can make it odd, even by stepping back.
step.defend: So far the side with the opposition was attacking; in this game it defends. The white king is on f3, the black king on f6, two squares in between, and So is to move. 55...Ke6 or 55...Kg6 would let the white king take the opposition and get in. So stepped back: 55...Kf7, three squares in between and White to move. The opposition is his, and it serves the defence.
step.d_carlsenSo: The moves of the game. For the white king's first three steps, So stays on the same file, three squares above.
step.d_carlsenSo.m1: 55...Kf7! He steps back and takes the distant opposition: f4, f5 and f6 in between, and White to move.
step.d_carlsenSo.m2: {{Carlsen|magnus-carlsen}} changes file, trying to get round the side.
step.d_carlsenSo.m3: 56...Ke7! So changes file with him: three squares in between again, now on the e-file.
step.d_carlsenSo.m4: {{Carlsen|magnus-carlsen}} tries the d-file. If So does not follow now, he loses: 57...Kd7 is again the only move.
step.d_carlsenSo.m5: 57...Kd7! Facing him again, from afar. The white king moves, but gains no ground.
step.d_carlsenSo.m6: {{Carlsen|magnus-carlsen}} goes up the c-file, to come in from the queenside.
step.d_carlsenSo.m7: 58...Ke6! The black king comes back close to the pawns, and the white king has no way in. The game was drawn on move 63.
step.defendMove: Now with a single pawn: take the distant opposition and, when the white king comes up, face him.
step.defendMove.hint:
Defending may require a retreat. Look for a square on the white king’s file that leaves an odd number of squares between the kings and White to move. If the pawn advances, check its key squares again.

The refutations are organized by decision. Each variation begins with an attempt that fails to preserve the objective; it is not the recommended line.

Decision 1
The defence must retreat to the correct distance. Moving closer or retreating too far lets the white king gain ground.
1...Kf6 2.Kf4 Kg6 3.Kg4. The side making the attempt loses against correct play.
1...Kf8 2.Kf4 Kf7 3.Kg5. The side making the attempt loses against correct play.

Decision 2
The opposition must adapt to the white king’s new file. There is more than one defence, but not every nearby square works.
2...Kf6 3.Kf4 Kg6 4.Kg4. The side making the attempt loses against correct play.
2...Kg7 3.Kf5 Kh6 4.g4. The side making the attempt loses against correct play.

Decision 3
After the pawn advance, occupying the key square matters more than keeping the previous distance.
3...Kf7 4.Kf5 Kg7 5.Kg5. The side making the attempt loses against correct play.
step.defendMove.done:
You preserved the objective. The demonstration illustrates this plan: the defense maintained the correct distance and followed the change of file. After the pawn advance, the key square determined the retreat.

The demonstrated line is 1...Kf7 2.Ke4 Ke6 3.g4 Kf6. An equivalent alternative may complete the practice before this sequence ends.
Also preserve the objective: 2...Kg6.
At the third decision, 3...Kf6 occupies the square needed for the defense.
part.lateral.title: Lateral opposition
part.lateral.summary: The opposition also works along a rank, near and far, in attack and in defence.
step.t_euwe: Now the kings face each other sideways. In The Hague in 1928, the World Amateur Championship was held alongside the Olympiad as a separate individual competition. In this game, {{Max Euwe|max-euwe}} had White against {{Norman Whitaker|norman-whitaker}}. The rooks were exchanged on move 47, leaving each side with one pawn. The struggle is to reach the opposing pawn first: your king is heading for a5, while the black king threatens to reach c2. Only one move wins. Which move is it?
step.t_euwe.hint1: The kings can face each other sideways, on the same rank.
step.t_euwe.hint2: Count the squares between the kings on the fifth rank after your move.
step.lateral: So far the kings faced each other head on or along the diagonal; {{Euwe|max-euwe}} used the rank. He played 49.Kb5: it attacks the a5-pawn and puts the kings on the fifth rank, three squares in between and Black to move. That is distant opposition along the rank: when the black king goes down towards the c2-pawn, the white king goes down with him, sideways, and gets there first.
step.d_euwe: The moves of the game: {{Euwe|max-euwe}} always stays on the black king's rank.
step.d_euwe.m1: 49.Kb5! The only winning move. Kings on b5 and f5, three squares in between, and Black to move.
step.d_euwe.m3: 50.Kxa5! The pawn falls, and the kings again have three squares in between, a5 and e5, with Black to move.
step.d_euwe.m4: He goes further down and threatens 51...Kc3, attacking the c2-pawn.
step.d_euwe.m5: 51.Kb4! Kings on b4 and d4, one square in between, and Black to move: lateral opposition, and c3 is shut to him.
step.d_euwe.m6: With no way through c3, he steps back. Every move loses: the white king is already in front of the pawn.
step.d_euwe.m7: 52.Kb5. The white king goes up in front of the pawn, towards b6 and c6. {{Euwe|max-euwe}} went on with 53.c4, 54.Kb6 and 55.Kc6, and the game ended there, a win for White.
step.lateralDefend: The white king will come down to support the d2-pawn; come down with him, sideways, and get there first.
step.lateralDefend.hint:
Count the distance along the rank. Follow the white king’s descent without allowing it to reach the key squares before you.

The refutations are organized by decision. Each variation begins with an attempt that fails to preserve the objective; it is not the recommended line.

Decision 1
The defending king needs to reach the same rank in time.
1...Ke7 2.Kb5 Kd6 3.Kc4. The side making the attempt loses against correct play.
1...Kf6 2.Kb5 Ke6 3.Kc5. The side making the attempt loses against correct play.

Decision 2
Lateral opposition prevents access to the key squares; a difference of one square can open the route.
2...Kd6 3.Kc4 Kc6 4.d3. The side making the attempt loses against correct play.
2...Ke5 3.Kc5 Kf5 4.d4. The side making the attempt loses against correct play.

Decision 3
Following along the rank keeps a barrier between the attacking king and the decisive squares.
3...Kd6 4.Kc4 Kc6 5.d3. The side making the attempt loses against correct play.
3...Ke4 4.Kc4 Ke5 5.Kc5. The side making the attempt loses against correct play.
step.lateralDefend.done:
You preserved the objective. The demonstration illustrates this plan: lateral opposition maintained a barrier in front of the decisive squares. Following along the rank can require retreating before facing the king.

The demonstrated line is 1...Ke6 2.Kb5 Kd5 3.Kb4 Kd4. An equivalent alternative may complete the practice before this sequence ends.
The replies 2...Kd5 and 3...Kd4 follow the change of rank and maintain the barrier.
part.capablanca.title: Capablanca's example
part.capablanca.summary: With blocked pawns on both wings, obtain opposition before choosing the route in.
step.t_capablanca: Locked pawns on both sides and the kings far apart. Whoever reaches an enemy pawn first wins. Think: which white king move makes sure of getting there first?
step.t_capablanca.hint1: Count the squares between the kings on the e-file. With an even number, the side to move can take the opposition.
step.t_capablanca.hint2: Six squares in between and your move: after your move an odd number must be left.
step.capablanca: Now there are pawns on both sides, and the target is not queening: it is the other side's pawn. This is the example {{Capablanca|jose-raul-capablanca}} chose, in Chess Fundamentals, to show the value of the opposition. Each side has two blocked pawns, b4 against b5 and h4 against h5, and the kings are on e1 and e8, with six squares between them. An even number: whoever is to move takes the opposition, and whoever takes the opposition wins, because he reaches the other side's pawn first. 1.Ke2 is the only move that wins.
step.d_capablanca: Watch distant opposition become direct. The preparation for outflanking will be examined in the next section.
step.d_capablanca.m1: 1.Ke2. Five squares in between, and Black to move.
step.d_capablanca.m2: The black king comes down the file.
step.d_capablanca.m3: 2.Ke3. Three squares in between, and he is still the one to move.
step.d_capablanca.m4: He comes forward again: two squares in between, and it is my move.
step.d_capablanca.m5: 3.Ke4. Direct opposition, one square in between: now Black has to leave the file.
step.capablancaMove: Take the distant opposition and, when the black king leaves the file, do not follow him: step forward on the other side and take the opposition again.
step.capablancaMove.hint:
First consider who will have to give way on the kings’ file. If the opposing king changes file, compare a diagonal step with approaching in a straight line: what matters is the opposition after its reply.

The refutations are organized by decision. Each variation begins with an attempt that fails to preserve the objective; it is not the recommended line.

Decision 1
The first step must establish distant opposition before choosing a wing.
1.Kd2 Kf7 2.Kc3 Ke6. The position allows a draw.
1.Kf2 Kd7 2.Ke3 Ke7. The position allows a draw.

Decision 2
The black king’s change of file requires recalculating the opposition after its reply.
2.Ke3 Ke7 3.Kd3 Kf6. The position allows a draw.
2.Kf3 Kf7 3.Ke3 Ke7. The position allows a draw.

Decision 3
After the lateral waiting move, it is time to return to the file at the correct distance.
3.Kd4 Kd6 4.Ke4 Ke6. The position allows a draw.
3.Ke4 Ke6 4.Kd4 Kf5. The position allows a draw.
step.capablancaMove.done:
You preserved the objective. The demonstration illustrates this plan: the lateral waiting move was followed by regaining distant opposition on the correct file. Gaining space does not mean advancing on every move.

The demonstrated line is 1.Ke2 Kf8 2.Kd3 Ke7 3.Ke3. An equivalent alternative may complete the practice before this sequence ends.
Also preserve the objective: 2.Kf2.
part.edge.title: Lateral approach
part.edge.summary: The squares controlled by the pawns show how to follow the opposing king.
step.t_edge: The goal is to win, and the target is the c6-pawn. 1.Kd6 looks like the shortest way. Is it?
step.t_edge.hint1: After 1.Kd6, where does the black king stand, and whose move is it?
step.t_edge.hint2: The kings are on the fifth rank; count the squares between them.
step.edge: In the previous chapter the outflanking happened in the middle of the board; now it happens at the edge. This is a training position on distant opposition. 1.Kd6? Kb6! and the kings stand side by side, one square in between, with White to move: the white king does not get through, and it is a draw. The right move is to step away: 1.Kf5. That leaves four squares in between, from a5 to f5, and Black to move, but the black king cannot stay on the fifth rank: b5 is covered by the c4-pawn. He has to go up, and I go up with him, three squares in between. Then the kings climb together, side by side, and at the top I use the edge to gain the move.
step.d_edge: Watch the kings climb side by side.
step.d_edge.m1: 1.Kf5! I step away: a5 and f5, four squares in between, and Black to move. The black king cannot answer on b5, which the c4-pawn covers.
step.d_edge.m2: The black king has to leave the fifth rank: b5 and b4 are covered by the c4- and a3-pawns. He goes up.
step.d_edge.m3: 2.Kf6. I go up with him: b6 and f6, three squares in between, and he is to move. The c6-pawn stands on one of them, but it counts just the same.
step.d_edge.m4: He goes up to b7, and I go up with him to keep three squares in between on the same rank.
step.d_edge.m5: 3.Kf7. Seventh rank, three squares in between, and he is still the one to move.
step.edgeMove: This time the black king answers differently.
step.edgeMove.hint:
The shortest route to the pawn may surrender the opposition. Observe the squares your pawns deny the opposing king and look for a way to keep a route in from the side.

The refutations are organized by decision. Each variation begins with an attempt that fails to preserve the objective; it is not the recommended line.

Decision 1
The closeness of c6 is misleading: access depends on opposition and the squares denied by the pawns.
1.Kd6 Kb6 2.Ke5 Ka7. The position allows a draw.
1.Ke4 Ka6 2.Kd3 Ka5. The position allows a draw.

Decision 2
After the black king goes to a6, the route in must be kept along the sixth rank. Returning to the fifth or fourth gives the defender time to reorganise the opposition.
2.Ke4 Kb6 3.Kd3 Ka5. The position allows a draw.
2.Ke5 Ka7 3.Ke4 Ka6. The position allows a draw.
2.Kg5 Ka7 3.Kf4 Ka6. The position allows a draw.

Decision 3
Going forward without counting the turn gives away lateral opposition; approaching along the rank preserves access.
3.Kd7 Kb7 4.Kd6 Kb6. The position allows a draw.
step.edgeMove.done:
You preserved the objective. The demonstration illustrates this plan: lateral opposition preserves access to c6. Distance from the target matters less than the entry squares available after the opponent’s reply.

The demonstrated line is 1.Kf5 Ka6 2.Ke6 Kb6 3.Kd6. An equivalent alternative may complete the practice before this sequence ends.
Also preserve the objective: 2.Kg6.
Also preserve the objective: 3.Kf6.
part.reserve.title: Spare tempo
part.reserve.summary: A free pawn move passes the turn and hands the opposition to the other side.
step.t_reserve: The black king has reached e7, with five squares between the kings, and White is to move. The extra pawn on a2 provides a reserve tempo. How can White preserve the win without treating opposition as an isolated counting rule?
step.t_reserve.hint1: Who has a move that changes nothing between the kings?
step.t_reserve.hint2: A pawn move passes the turn, and the turn decides the opposition.
step.reserve: A reserve tempo is a move that can change whose turn it is without moving the kings. Here, 1.a3 preserves the win: the white king remains on e1 and the black king on e7, but Black must now move. In the line 1...Ke6 2.Ke2 Ke5 3.Ke3, the white king then reduces the distance. Other continuations also win; consider the reserve before concluding that the king must give way.
step.d_reserve: Watch the spare tempo hand the opposition over.
step.d_reserve.m1: 1.a3. The pawn passes the move without moving the kings. Black is to move with five squares between them.
step.d_reserve.m2: 1...Ke6. The black king advances. There are now four squares between the kings, with White to move.
step.d_reserve.m3: 2.Ke2. The king reduces the distance, leaving three squares between the kings with Black to move. Here, this is the only winning move.
step.d_reserve.m4: 2...Ke5. The black king advances again; two squares separate the kings.
step.d_reserve.m5: 3.Ke3. White takes direct opposition. The black king must give way, allowing the outflanking maneuver studied in Capablanca’s example.
step.grigorievMove: Now apply the correct order of waiting moves. The goal is still to win, but the king must not take away the opponent’s squares too early.
step.grigorievMove.hint:
Count the advances each side can use to pass the move. Bringing the king closer too early can remove every opposing square and cause stalemate; advancing a pawn too early can allow an exchange. Seek a waiting move that preserves your reserves and forces the opponent to spend theirs.

The refutations are organized by decision. Each variation begins with an attempt that fails to preserve the objective; it is not the recommended line.

Decision 1
The order begins with the pawn structure: moving the king first or spending both advances allows a draw.
1.Kb8 b4 2.cxb4 Kb5. The position allows a draw.
1.b4 Ka6 2.Kb8 Kb6. The position allows a draw.

Decision 2
Waiting with the king preserves both the pawn reserve and the opponent’s escape squares. Approaching too early can cause stalemate; advancing a pawn too early spends the reserve or allows a capture.
2.Ka7 b4 3.c4. The position allows a draw.
2.Kb7 b4 3.c4. The position allows a draw.
2.b4+ Ka6 3.Kb8 Kb6. The position allows a draw.
2.c4 bxc4 3.bxc4 Ka4. The position allows a draw.

Decision 3
Capturing simplifies away the advantage; advancing without capturing keeps both pawns and passes the move.
3.cxb4+ Kxb4 4.Ka7 Kxb3. The position allows a draw.
step.grigorievMove.done:
You preserved the objective. The demonstration illustrates this plan: the waiting move preserves your reserves and the opposing squares needed to avoid stalemate. Only after the opponent spends their own tempo is it appropriate to change the structure.

The demonstrated line is 1.b3 Ka5 2.Kb8 b4 3.c4. An equivalent alternative may complete the practice before this sequence ends.
part.means.title: Choose the target
part.means.summary: The opposition is there to reach the key square or the pawn. If you can get there without it, do.
step.t_means: 1.Ke4 takes direct opposition. Is it the move?
step.t_means.hint1: Where are the key squares of the c4-pawn? Can you reach them without going through the opposition?
step.means: Opposition helps to gain space, but the decision should begin with the objective. Here, 1.Ke4 takes the opposition but only draws after 1...Kd6. The advance 1.Kc5 preserves the win because it brings the king closer to the key squares b6, c6 and d6. First ask where the king needs to go; then choose the technique that takes it there.
step.d_means: Watch the white king go straight to the key square.
step.d_means.m1: 1.Kc5! No opposition at all: the king goes to the door, with b6 and d6 within reach.
step.d_means.m2: The black king tries to block from the d-side.
step.d_means.m3: 2.Kb6. A key square of the c4-pawn. From here the pawn queens.
step.d_means.m4: He goes in front of the pawn.
step.d_means.m5: 3.Kc6. I take away b7, c7 and d7: the black king only has the eighth rank.
step.d_means.m6: He only has b8 and d8. He goes to b8, and c8 is within my king's reach.
step.d_means.m7: 4.Kd7. I control c8, and the pawn walks to queen on its own.
step.recap:
Take three questions into your games. First: what is the king’s objective — reach a key square, capture a target, or prevent the opponent from entering? Second: whose move is it, and which pawn reserves can still change the turn? Third: should you follow, wait, or outflank? Opposition organises the struggle for space, but it is useful only when it serves the objective. In defence, a fixed target on the other wing can also create counterplay.

Also compare the purpose of the pawn advances studied. In the reserve practices, playing h5–h6 early allows a draw when White needs to win: the king must still capture the blocker. In the 1920 study, fixing a5 comes first because it removes a black reserve that would change the timing of the defense. In the 1929 study in the final test, fixing h7 creates a target for counterplay, but the king must be prepared first. There is therefore no fixed order of pawn before king or king before pawn: the advance’s purpose and the opponent’s reply determine its timing. In lateral defense, it may also be necessary to retreat first to reach the appropriate rank.
step.finish: Now play until you queen. Your pawn is far from the kings: find the distant opposition, follow the black king and take yours to the key squares of the f2-pawn.
ex.e09: The black king stands in front of the key squares and yours is in the corner. Find the winning move.
ex.e09.hint:
First the black king's file, from afar. Then, every time he moves, shorten the distance facing him.

The refutations are organized by decision. Each variation begins with an attempt that fails to preserve the objective; it is not the recommended line.

Decision 1
The king is still in the corner: advancing the pawn before bringing the king out lets the defender occupy the centre.
1.d3 Kf7 2.d4 Ke6. The position allows a draw.
1.d4 Kf7 2.d5 Kf6. The position allows a draw.

Decision 2
The approach must shorten the distance; staying back on the second rank lets the black king establish its defence.
2.Kf2 Ke6 3.d3 Kd5. The position allows a draw.

Decision 3
The king needs to advance with opposition, not merely change file while keeping the wrong distance.
3.Ke3 Ke5 4.d3 Kd5. The position allows a draw.

Decision 4
The king must still be placed correctly before spending a pawn advance.
4.d3 Ke6 5.d4 Kd6. The position allows a draw.
4.d4 Ke6 5.d5+ Kd6. The position allows a draw.
ex.e09.solution:
1.Kg2! takes the distant opposition on the g-file, with five squares in between. After 1...Kf7, 2.Kf3! After 2...Ke6, 3.Ke4! And after 3...Kd6, 4.Kd4! Every step keeps the number odd, down to direct opposition beside the pawn. Starting with the pawn or with another king move draws.

Why other attempts fail:

Decision 1: The king is still in the corner: advancing the pawn before bringing the king out lets the defender occupy the centre. 1.d3 1...Kf7 2.d4 2...Ke6: allows a draw. 1.d4 1...Kf7 2.d5 2...Kf6: allows a draw.

Decision 2: The approach must shorten the distance; staying back on the second rank lets the black king establish its defence. 2.Kf2 2...Ke6 3.d3 3...Kd5: allows a draw.

Decision 3: The king needs to advance with opposition, not merely change file while keeping the wrong distance. 3.Ke3 3...Ke5 4.d3 4...Kd5: allows a draw.

key.lesson: The white king takes the opposition from far away, with several squares between the kings, and closes the gap step by step until it reaches the deciding squares in front of the pawn.
key.diagonal: The opposition works along the diagonal too: the white king stands on the same diagonal as the black king and, step by step, turns it into face-to-face opposition.
key.means: The opposition is a means, not the goal: here taking it only draws. What wins is taking the king straight to the deciding squares in front of the pawn.
key.capablanca: {{Capablanca|jose-raul-capablanca}}'s example: locked pawns on both sides and the kings far apart. Whoever is to move takes the distant opposition and wins.
key.carlsenSo: {{Carlsen|magnus-carlsen}} against So, {{Norway Chess|norway-chess}}, {{Stavanger|stavanger}}, 2017. So was a pawn down and defending. His king stepped back to take the opposition from afar and followed the white king from file to file until the draw.
key.euweWhitaker: {{Euwe|max-euwe}} against {{Whitaker|norman-whitaker}}, The Hague, 1928. The white king took the opposition from afar, sideways, on the same rank as the black king, and reached the pawn that mattered first: White won.
history: Opposition is the contest between kings to force the opponent to give up space. It can begin at a distance, with several squares between the kings, or along a diagonal. The goal is not merely to obtain that relationship: it is to reach an important square, capture a pawn, or prevent an opposing entry. In his 1921 book Chess Fundamentals, {{José Raúl Capablanca|jose-raul-capablanca}} presents the topic through pawn-ending examples. The technique also appears in high-level games: at Norway Chess in Stavanger in 2017, {{Wesley So|wesley-so}} defended an ending a pawn down against {{Magnus Carlsen|magnus-carlsen}} by following the opposing king from a distance. The game ended in a draw. The apparent simplicity of the pieces conceals a precise contest for space and time.
practice: Now the real ending: king on h3, pawn on f3, and the black king on e6, in front of the key squares. Find the diagonal, turn it into direct opposition and queen the pawn. Pick your pace and go.

Decision 1
An immediate approach does not preserve the win: Black follows along the edge and continues to prevent a decisive entry. The waiting move must prepare the next opposition.
1.Ke6 Ka6 2.Ke5 Ka7. The position allows a draw.
1.Ke7 Ka7 2.Kd6 Kb6. The position allows a draw.

Decision 2
After Black’s reply, switching to the d-file abandons the correct relationship between the kings. Black can follow; approaching the target without controlling the entry allows a draw.
2.Kd7 Kb7 3.Kd6 Kb6. The position allows a draw.
2.Kd8 Kb8 3.Kd7 Kb7. The position allows a draw.
step.edgeCornerMove.done:
You preserved the objective. The demonstration illustrates this plan: at the edge, the waiting move prepares new opposition. The king preserves access to the target with the correct turn, even when it first needs to move away.

The demonstrated line is 1.Ke8 Ka7 2.Ke7. An equivalent alternative may complete the practice before this sequence ends.
Also preserve the objective: 1.Kf6, 1.Kf8.
step.reserveMove: Black has just taken distant opposition. Preserve White’s win by using the reserve at the right moment, then bring the king closer.
step.reserveMove.hint:
A reserve can change whose turn it is without moving the kings. Once it has served that purpose, another advance may allow capture by the b-pawn. Compare the opposition obtained by each king approach; stepping sideways may return the favorable turn to the opponent.

The refutations are organized by decision. Each variation begins with an attempt that fails to preserve the objective; it is not the recommended line.

Decision 2
The reserve has already served its purpose. Another pawn advance allows capture by the b-pawn, while leaving the correct file lets the black king regain opposition. The king must now approach at the correct distance.
2.a4 bxa4 3.Kd1 a3. The position allows a draw.
2.Kd2 Kd6 3.a4 bxa4. The position allows a draw.
2.Kf2 Kd5 3.Ke2 Kc4. The position allows a draw.

Decision 3
On the final approach, a sideways deviation lets the black king follow. Preserving the win requires converting distant opposition into direct opposition without spending another reserve at the wrong time.
3.Kd3 Kd5 4.a4 bxa4. The position allows a draw.
3.Kf3 Kf5 4.Ke2 Ke4. The position allows a draw.
step.reserveMove.done:
You preserved the objective. The demonstration illustrates this plan: the reserve changes whose turn it is without moving the kings. The approach then converts distant opposition into direct opposition. The reserve’s value depends on the position, not merely on having a pawn move.

The demonstrated line is 1.a3 Ke6 2.Ke2 Ke5 3.Ke3. An equivalent alternative may complete the practice before this sequence ends.
Also preserve the objective: 1.Kd1, 1.Kd2, 1.Ke2, 1.Kf1, 1.Kf2.
Also preserve the objective: 3.Ke1.
step.d_waiting.m1: 1.b3. The advance preserves the two-pawn structure and prepares the waiting plan. Spending both steps at once would allow a draw.
step.d_waiting.m2: 1...Ka5. The black king moves to the edge and keeps its pawn advance available. It is not yet time to bring the white king closer.
step.d_waiting.m3: 2.Kb8. This is the king’s waiting move: it stays close without taking away the opponent’s squares too early. Approaching now can allow stalemate after the pawn advances.
step.d_waiting.m4: 2...b4. Black spends its reserve. Only now is it useful to employ the waiting move of White’s other pawn.
step.d_waiting.m5: 3.c4. The pawn passes the move without capturing. The win remains, and the black king still has squares: the reserve worked because the king’s approach was delayed.
part.waiting.title: Waiting with kings
part.waiting.summary: Before using the pawn reserve, it may be necessary to wait with the king.
step.t_waiting: In this study attributed to {{Nikolai Grigoriev|nikolai-grigoriev}}, from 1930, White must win with two pawns against one. The king is already close, but bringing it closer too quickly may help the defence. How should the king’s and pawns’ waiting moves be coordinated?
step.t_waiting.hint1: Compare how many advances each side can still make without moving its king.
step.t_waiting.hint2: A king that comes too close can also take away every square from an opponent that is not in check. Keep a waiting move before bringing it closer.
step.waiting: In the previous example, the main idea was changing the turn with a pawn. Here the order needs more care. After 1.b3 Ka5, 2.Kb8 waits with the king. If it approaches with 2.Ka7? b4 3.c4, Black has no legal move and is not in check: that is stalemate, and therefore a draw. In the winning line, 2...b4 3.c4 passes the move while the white king is still farther away. Waiting is not wasting time: it preserves the conditions needed to use the reserve.
step.d_waiting: Observe three stages: prepare the pawn structure, wait with the king, and only then pass the move with the other pawn.
step.meansMove: Win this position by choosing the objective before the form of opposition. Aim to place the king on a key square.
step.meansMove.hint:
Compare a square that merely faces the other king with one that brings you closer to the goal. If the pawn advances without support, the opposing king can catch it; prepare its promotion before pushing it.

The refutations are organized by decision. Each variation begins with an attempt that fails to preserve the objective; it is not the recommended line.

Decision 1
Advancing the pawn before the king allows it to be caught and captured. The key square serves the concrete goal of supporting promotion.
1.c5 Kd7 2.c6+ Kxc6. The position allows a draw.
step.meansMove.done:
You preserved the win. In the demonstrated line, 2.Kb6 reaches a key square to support promotion. The alternatives 2.Kb5 and 2.Kd5 also preserve the win, but do not reach a key square on that move: each requires its own continuation.

The demonstrated line is 1.Kc5 Kd7 2.Kb6. An equivalent alternative may complete the practice before this sequence ends.
Also preserve the objective: 2.Kb5, 2.Kd5.
part.fixedTarget.title: Fix first
part.fixedTarget.summary: Fix the distant pawn before organizing the king’s defensive route.
step.t_fixedTarget: In this 1920 study by Grigoriev, the black king threatens to capture h3 and support a passed pawn. White must also consider the other wing. Which first move preserves the draw?
step.t_fixedTarget.hint1: Before starting the king’s race, examine the pawn moves Black can still keep in reserve.
step.t_fixedTarget.hint2: A blocked pawn loses its freedom to advance. That difference in timing matters when the kings must face each other.
step.fixedTarget: 1.a4 is the only move that draws. It fixes the pawn on a5: Black no longer has an advance on that wing to change whose turn it is when the kings face each other. After 1...Kg3 2.Ke6 Kxh3 3.Kf5, White has given up h3 but retained a defensive route. Fixation prepares that route; White must still coordinate precisely with the king and the black pawn’s advances.
step.d_fixedTarget: Observe the order: first block the distant reserve, then bring the king to the defense.
step.fixedTargetMove: Preserve the draw from the beginning of the study: prepare the pawn structure, then organize the king’s route.
step.fixedTargetMove.hint:
An immediate king race leaves the opponent a resource on the other wing. Remove that resource before bringing the king closer.

The refutations are organized by decision. Each variation begins with an attempt that fails to preserve the objective; it is not the recommended line.

Decision 1
Fixation comes before the race: without it, Black retains the distant reserve and can combine play on both sides of the board.
1.Kc6 Kg3 2.Kb5 Kxh3. The side making the attempt loses against correct play.
1.Kd6 Kg3 2.Ke5 Kxh3. The side making the attempt loses against correct play.
1.Ke6 a4 2.Kd5 h5. The side making the attempt loses against correct play.

Decision 2
After fixation, diverting the king to the queenside or advancing h3 leaves the black king an effective route to support the passed pawn. The defense requires reaching the kingside in time.
2.Kc6 Kxh3 3.Kb5 h5. The side making the attempt loses against correct play.
2.h4 Kxh4 3.Kc6 h5. The side making the attempt loses against correct play.

Decision 3
The king must reach a square from which it can coordinate with the next advance. The deviations to d5 or f6 do not prepare that coordination and lose.
3.Kd5 h5 4.Ke4 Kg3. The side making the attempt loses against correct play.
3.Kf6 h5 4.Ke5 h4. The side making the attempt loses against correct play.
step.fixedTargetMove.done:
You preserved the objective. The demonstration illustrates this plan: in this study, fixing the distant reserve prepares the defensive route. Losing h3 does not decide the result: the defense depends on coordinating the king with Black’s moves.

The demonstrated line is 1.a4 Kg3 2.Ke6 Kxh3 3.Kf5. An equivalent alternative may complete the practice before this sequence ends.
step.err_distantKing.m1: 1...Ke7. The black king occupies the same file, with three squares between the kings and White to move.
step.err_distantKing.m2: 2.g4. The pawn advance changes the turn but does not take the white king to a key square.
step.err_distantKing.m3: 2...Ke6. The black king shortens the distance and retains a sufficient defence. The win was lost with the white king’s first step.
step.err_distantKing: The white king has come only as far as e3. Watch how the defence organises the opposition.
step.err_distantPawn.m1: 1...Kd7. The black king approaches through the centre while the white king remains behind the pawn.
step.err_distantPawn.m2: 2.g5. The next advance gains ground for the pawn but does not solve its king’s insufficient position.
step.err_distantPawn.m3: 2...Kd6. The king reaches the centre in time to defend. Advancing the pawn did not replace preparation with the king.
step.err_distantPawn: The white pawn advanced before its king gained space. Observe the defender’s central route.
step.err_diagonalKing.m1: 1...Ke6. Black faces the opposing king, with one square between them and White to move.
step.err_diagonalKing.m2: 2.Kd3. The white king must look for another route; the direct approach did not secure a way through.
step.err_diagonalKing.m3: 2...Kd5. The defence follows onto the new file and keeps direct opposition. The position is drawn.
step.err_diagonalKing: The white king chose the direct entry on e4. Follow the opposition obtained by Black.
step.err_diagonalCheck.m1: 1...Ke6. The king escapes the check and continues preventing entry in front of the pawn.
step.err_diagonalCheck.m2: 2.e5. The pawn advances again. The white king has still not established a winning position.
step.err_diagonalCheck.m3: 2...Kd7. The king retreats safely; the defence preserves the draw. The active-looking check did not compensate for missing the key square.
step.err_diagonalCheck: The white pawn has just given check, but the king did not occupy the available key square. See why the check is not decisive.
step.err_defendClose.m1: 1.Kf4. White takes direct opposition, with Black to move.
step.err_defendClose.m2: 1...Kg6. The black king gives way on the file. White already has a winning continuation.
step.err_defendClose.m3: 2.Kg4. The white king follows and maintains opposition, preparing to enter the key squares.
step.err_defendClose: Black brought the king closer too early. Now follow White, which can gain space.
step.err_defendRetreat.m1: 1.Kf5. The white king reaches a key square for the pawn and preserves the win.
step.err_defendRetreat.m2: 1...Kg7. The black king tries to stay in front, but has already conceded a decisive position.
step.err_defendRetreat.m3: 2.Kg5. The white king occupies another key square and keeps the winning position.
step.err_defendRetreat: Black retreated when it needed to guard the key squares. Watch the white king enter.
step.err_lateralFile.m1: 1.Kb5. The white king descends towards the important squares for supporting its pawn.
step.err_lateralFile.m2: 1...Ke6. Black tries to correct the route, but White already has time to advance.
step.err_lateralFile.m3: 2.Kc5. The white king gains ground. The defence arrived too late to maintain the lateral barrier.
step.err_lateralFile: The black king moved down without adjusting its file. Now follow the space gained by White.
step.err_lateralDistance.m1: 1.Kc4. The white king reaches a key square for the d2-pawn.
step.err_lateralDistance.m2: 1...Kc6. The black king tries to obtain opposition on the file, but the important entry has already happened.
step.err_lateralDistance.m3: 2.d3. The pawn advances with support from its king’s position. White’s advantage remains winning.
step.err_lateralDistance: The black king kept the wrong distance along the rank. Follow White’s entry.
step.err_capablanca.m1: 1...Ke7. Black returns to the e-file with three squares between the kings and White to move.
step.err_capablanca.m2: 2.Kd3. The white king changes direction, but can no longer force the same route through.
step.err_capablanca.m3: 2...Kf6. The defence can reorganise on the other wing. The position remains drawn despite the white king’s apparent initiative.
step.err_capablanca: The white king advanced straight ahead after the opposing king changed file. See who obtains the opposition.
step.err_edge.m1: 1...Kb6. The black king takes lateral opposition: one square between the kings, with White to move.
step.err_edge.m2: 2.Ke5. The white king turns back to look for another route. The earlier approach did not secure the capture.
step.err_edge.m3: 2...Ka7. The black king maintains a sufficient defence. Access to the pawn has not been won.
step.err_edge: The white king rushed directly to d6. The pawn looks close, but opposition determines access.
step.err_waitStalemate.m1: 1...b4. Black advances the pawn and prepares a position with no available king moves.
step.err_waitStalemate.m2: 2.c4. Black now has no legal move and is not in check: it is stalemate. The position is drawn immediately.
step.err_waitStalemate: The white king approached a7 before Black’s reserve was spent. Observe the stalemate resource.
step.err_waitCapture.m1: 1...Kxb4. The black king captures the pawn that came to b4.
step.err_waitCapture.m2: 2.Ka7. The white king approaches but cannot protect the last pawn.
step.err_waitCapture.m3: 2...Kxb3. The last white pawn is captured. Only the kings remain: a draw.
step.err_waitCapture: White captured instead of passing the move with the pawn. See what remains after the simplification.
part.secondReserve.title: Save a tempo
part.secondReserve.summary: Keep the second advance for when the king’s route needs a change of turn.
step.t_secondReserve: The black king is near the queenside pawns, and White’s c2-pawn can still advance one or two squares. There are also pawns on the h-file, which change the kings’ routes. How can you advance without spending a reserve you may need later?
step.t_secondReserve.hint1: Two one-square advances change the turn twice; one double advance does so only once.
step.t_secondReserve.hint2: Besides the distance between the kings, observe the sixth-rank square controlled by Black’s h7-pawn.
step.secondReserve: The advance 1.c3 preserves the win and keeps the second step available. By contrast, 1.c4 allows a draw: the pawn uses in one go the space that could provide two waiting moves. After 1.c3 Ke4 2.Kg5 Ke5, the h7-pawn prevents the white king from continuing through g6. It is time to change the turn: 3.c4 preserves the win, whereas 3.h6 allows a draw. The criterion is the actual position. In the edge section, the limit came from the end of the board; here, a square controlled by a pawn also forces a change of plan.
step.d_secondReserve: Observe when the second advance is kept in reserve and when it becomes useful.
step.d_secondReserve.m1: 1.c3. The pawn advances only one square. It leaves c2 without spending the advance to c4, which can change the turn later.
step.d_secondReserve.m2: 1...Ke4. The black king advances and tries to keep facing its opponent along the rank.
step.d_secondReserve.m3: 2.Kg5. The white king follows upwards and keeps the win. The c3-pawn remains available as a reserve.
step.d_secondReserve.m4: 2...Ke5. The kings stand on the same rank with one square between them and White to move. Progress up the g-file is restricted by the h7-pawn.
step.d_secondReserve.m5: 3.c4. The reserve changes the turn at the useful moment. The black king must choose a reply, and White preserves a winning route to the h7 target.
step.secondReserveMove: Manage the reserve: preserve the win while the kings’ positions and the h7-pawn determine when to spend the second advance.
step.secondReserveMove.hint:
Compare what changes when a pawn advances one or two squares. Before moving the king up, check the squares controlled by pawns. Fixing the target too early may also allow an opposing central advance: spend the reserve when it improves the position.

The refutations are organized by decision. Each variation begins with an attempt that fails to preserve the objective; it is not the recommended line.

Decision 3
Fixing h7 with the pawn now allows 3...c4: Black’s central resource changes the structure before the target is captured.
3.h6 c4 4.Kg4 Ke4. The position allows a draw.
step.secondReserveMove.done:
You preserved the objective. The demonstration illustrates this plan: keeping the second advance in reserve means waiting until it improves the position. The reserve and the squares controlled by the h7-pawn determine the order of actions.

The demonstrated line is 1.c3 Ke4 2.Kg5 Ke5 3.c4. An equivalent alternative may complete the practice before this sequence ends.
Also preserve the objective: 1.Kf5, 1.Kg5.
Also preserve the objective: 2.b3, 2.b4, 2.Kh4.
Also preserve the objective: 3.b3, 3.b4, 3.Kg4, 3.Kh4, 3.Kh6.
step.d_useReserve: After using the reserve, turn the change in the position into a concrete target. Move numbering restarts in this diagram; this is a winning continuation.
step.d_useReserve.m1: 1.Kh6. The white king approaches h7 through h6, avoiding g6, which the black pawn controls.
step.d_useReserve.m2: 1...Kd3. The black king continues its plan to capture on the other wing. White retains the advantage in the race between the targets.
step.d_useReserve.m3: 2.Kxh7. The h7 target is captured. White’s h-pawn can advance.
step.d_useReserve.m4: 2...Kxc4. Black also captures a pawn, but this reply does not eliminate White’s win.
step.d_useReserve.m5: 3.h6. Now the pawn advance serves promotion. Earlier, the correct reserve had to be preserved; after capturing the blocker, the objective has changed.
step.d_useReserve.m6: 3...Kb3. The black king continues on the queenside. White retains a winning position with the h-pawn free.
step.err_reserve_early_c4: White spent both advances of the c2-pawn at once. Observe Black’s approach to the base of the pawns.
step.err_reserve_early_c4.m1: 1...Kd3. The black king changes direction and approaches the queenside pawns.
step.err_reserve_early_c4.m2: 2.b3. The advance tries to reorganise the structure, but the c-pawn’s reserve has already been spent.
step.err_reserve_early_c4.m3: 2...Kc2. The black king approaches the base of the pawns and retains enough resources to draw.
step.err_reserve_early_c4.m4: 3.b4. The pawn advances, but the position remains drawn. The space gained by the double advance did not replace the tempo that was lost.
step.err_reserve_early_h6: In this position, White advanced the h-pawn instead of using the c-file reserve. Observe Black’s central resource.
step.err_reserve_early_h6.m1: 1...c4. Black advances its own pawn. The blockade changes the queenside struggle before the white king can capture h7.
step.err_reserve_early_h6.m2: 2.Kg4. The white king turns back, but no longer has the same winning continuation.
step.err_reserve_early_h6.m3: 2...Ke4. The black king approaches and preserves equality. Fixing h7 now did not compensate for the central resource.
step.err_reserve_early_h6.m4: 3.Kg3. The white king tries to reorganise. The position remains drawn: a reserve useful in another position can be premature here.
part.useReserve.title: Use the reserve
part.useReserve.summary: After changing the turn, choose the target and route that preserve the win.
step.t_useReserve: The reserve has been used, and the black king has moved down to d4. The white king needs to turn this change into a concrete threat. Which route reaches the h7-pawn without crossing a square it controls?
step.t_useReserve.hint1: A pawn controls the diagonals in front of it, not the square immediately ahead.
step.t_useReserve.hint2: Compare the route along the g-file with approaching on the pawn’s own file.
step.useReserve: The reserve fulfilled its purpose because it created a useful continuation. Here, 1.Kh6 approaches the blocker from the front, avoiding g6, which the h7-pawn controls. After 1...Kd3, 2.Kxh7 removes the blocker. Even after 2...Kxc4, 3.h6 preserves the win. The pawn advance now serves promotion; earlier, the task was to manage the turn.
step.useReserveMove: Preserve the win by choosing the route to the target and, after the capture, the promotion plan.
step.useReserveMove.hint:
Check pawn control before choosing the king’s route. Advancing your own pawn before capturing the blocker may give time for captures on the other wing. Once the blocker is gone, reconsider whether keeping the advance in reserve is still necessary.

The refutations are organized by decision. Each variation begins with an attempt that fails to preserve the objective; it is not the recommended line.

Decision 1
The king’s route and the pawn advance are not interchangeable. Fixing h7 early allows captures on the queenside; the king’s approach preserves the win. Another tempo with the b-pawn is also sufficient.
1.h6 Kxc4 2.b3+ Kxb3. The position allows a draw.
step.useReserveMove.done:
You preserved the objective. The demonstration illustrates this plan: the goal changes during conversion: first capture the blocker, then promote. When to spend the reserve follows that plan.

The demonstrated line is 1.Kh6 Kd3 2.Kxh7 Kxc4 3.h6. An equivalent alternative may complete the practice before this sequence ends.
Also preserve the objective: 1.b3.
Also preserve the objective: 2.b3, 2.Kg7.
Also preserve the objective: 3.Kg6, 3.Kg7, 3.Kg8, 3.Kh6, 3.Kh8.
step.d_fixedTarget.m1: 1.a4. The pawn on a5 is blocked. Fixation removes a resource Black could use to change whose turn it is.
step.d_fixedTarget.m2: 1...Kg3. The black king attacks h3. White needs a precise route rather than to preserve every pawn.
step.d_fixedTarget.m3: 2.Ke6. The king uses the diagonal to reach f5 in time.
step.d_fixedTarget.m4: 2...Kxh3. Black captures h3. The position remains drawn: the white king can organize the defense against the passed pawn.
step.d_fixedTarget.m5: 3.Kf5. The king reaches the defensive area. In the next part, we will see how to meet the h-pawn’s advance.
part.synchronize.title: Coordinate the defense
part.synchronize.summary: Fixation allows the king to follow along the appropriate rank and stop the passed pawn.
step.t_synchronize: Black has just advanced the pawn to h5. The a5-pawn is already fixed, and the defense depends on the kings’ timing. Which retreat preserves the draw? The move numbering restarts from this diagram.
step.t_synchronize.hint1: Do not calculate only the distance to the pawn. Compare the ranks the kings can occupy after its next advance.
step.t_synchronize.hint2: Prepare a position where the kings face each other from the side, with the opponent to move.
step.synchronize: 1.Kf4 h4 2.Kf3 places the kings on f3 and h3, with one square between them and Black to move: this is lateral opposition. After 2...Kh2, 3.Kf2 preserves that relationship on the second rank. The advance 3...h3 controls g2; 4.Kf1 prepares the response without entering that square. Fixation on the a-file matters because Black cannot use an advance there to change whose turn it is.
step.d_synchronize: Follow the kings’ ranks. Each retreat prepares useful opposition after the opponent’s reply.
step.d_synchronize.m1: 1.Kf4. The king retreats to coordinate the defense rather than racing directly toward the pawn.
step.d_synchronize.m2: 1...h4. The pawn advances and now controls g3.
step.d_synchronize.m3: 2.Kf3. The kings stand on f3 and h3. Black is to move: lateral opposition prevents the black king from crossing g3.
step.d_synchronize.m4: 2...Kh2. The black king changes rank. White must follow that change.
step.d_synchronize.m5: 3.Kf2. Lateral opposition reappears on f2 and h2, with Black to move.
step.d_synchronize.m6: 3...h3. The pawn advances again and controls g2. The defense must respect that attacked square.
step.d_synchronize.m7: 4.Kf1. The king retreats to the first rank. The continuation will show how to regain opposition and block the pawn.
step.d_synchronizeFinish: Continue the defense until the passed pawn is captured. This new diagram begins with Black to move.
step.d_synchronizeFinish.m1: 1...Kg3. The black king reaches the g-file. The white king can respond on the same file.
step.d_synchronizeFinish.m2: 2.Kg1. The kings stand on g1 and g3, with Black to move: the opposition is now direct.
step.d_synchronizeFinish.m3: 2...Kf3. The black king leaves the g-file, allowing White to approach through h2.
step.d_synchronizeFinish.m4: 3.Kh2. The king blocks the pawn. The initial fixation and the sequence of oppositions made it possible to arrive in time.
step.d_synchronizeFinish.m5: 3...Ke3. The black king seeks activity on the other wing but can no longer prevent the capture on h3.
step.d_synchronizeFinish.m6: 4.Kxh3. The passed pawn has been eliminated. The position remains drawn; the a-pawns are still on the board.
step.synchronizeMove: Defend the draw by coordinating with the pawn advances and the black king’s changes of rank.
step.synchronizeMove.hint:
Choose the retreat by the opposition it prepares, rather than just by proximity to the pawn. Respect the squares controlled by the pawn.

The refutations are organized by decision. Each variation begins with an attempt that fails to preserve the objective; it is not the recommended line.

Decision 1
The approach through g5 and the deviation to e4 lose because they do not prepare the defense on the correct rank.
1.Ke4 Kg3 2.Kd3 h4. The side making the attempt loses against correct play.
1.Kg5 h4 2.Kf4 Kg2. The side making the attempt loses against correct play.

Decision 2
At this decision, moving away to e3 or up to g5 lets the black king enter through g3. Lateral opposition must prevent that passage.
2.Ke3 Kg3 3.Kd2 h3. The side making the attempt loses against correct play.
2.Kg5 Kg3 3.Kf5 h3. The side making the attempt loses against correct play.

Decision 3
The black king has changed rank. Moving upward again fails to follow that change and allows the pawn to advance with support.
3.Kg4 h3 4.Kf3 Kg1. The side making the attempt loses against correct play.

Decision 4
The pawn controls g2. Returning to the third rank abandons the defense along the first; the black king can support the next advance.
4.Kf3 Kg1 5.Ke3 h2. The side making the attempt loses against correct play.
step.synchronizeMove.done:
You preserved the objective. The demonstration illustrates this plan: the defense follows along the correct rank, alternating lateral and direct opposition until the pawn is stopped. The initial fixation made this coordination possible. In another structure, the purpose of fixation may require a different order.

The demonstrated line is 1.Kf4 h4 2.Kf3 Kh2 3.Kf2 h3 4.Kf1. An equivalent alternative may complete the practice before this sequence ends.
step.err_fixedTarget: White has just moved the king to e6, starting the race before fixing a5. See how Black uses the distant advance and preserves the win.
step.err_fixedTarget.m1: 1...a4. Black uses the advance that fixation would have prevented.
step.err_fixedTarget.m2: 2.Kd5. The white king seeks a central defense, but the position is already lost against correct play.
step.err_fixedTarget.m3: 2...h5. The other pawn advances too. White must cope with resources on both wings.
step.err_fixedTarget.m4: 3.Kd4. The king continues its approach; activity alone does not restore the draw.
step.err_fixedTarget.m5: 3...Kg3. Black attacks h3 with a winning position. The order of fixation and the king’s approach was decisive.
step.err_synchronize: White has just moved the king to g5, bringing it closer without preparing the defensive rank. See how the pawn advances with support from the black king.
step.err_synchronize.m1: 1...h4. The pawn gains space while the white king is still on the fifth rank.
step.err_synchronize.m2: 2.Kf4. The white king retreats but has not reached the third rank when lateral opposition would be needed.
step.err_synchronize.m3: 2...Kg2. The black king reaches the second rank and preserves the win. The approach through g5 did not prevent this entry.
step.err_synchronize.m4: 3.Ke3. The white king tries to return to the defense but has not recovered an effective barrier.
step.err_synchronize.m5: 3...h3. The pawn advances supported by the king on g2. Black remains winning: coordination was lost before this approach.
step.t_fixedTarget.hint3:
Starting the king’s race leaves Black the a-file reserve. Even when it is not used immediately, its availability changes the coordination of the defense. Prepare the structure before the route.

1.Kc6 Kg3 2.Kb5 Kxh3: White loses against correct play.

1.Kd6 Kg3 2.Ke5 Kxh3: White loses against correct play.

1.Ke6 a4 2.Kd5 h5: White loses against correct play.
step.t_synchronize.hint3:
Being closer to the pawn or seeking the center is not enough. These deviations fail to prepare the rank on which the king must face its opponent after the advance.

1.Ke4 Kg3 2.Kd3 h4: White loses against correct play.

1.Kg5 h4 2.Kf4 Kg2: White loses against correct play.
step.t_carlsenSo.hint3: Stepping sideways abandons the opposition relationship and allows the white king to advance with its pawns. Both 55...Ke5 56.Ke3 Kd5 57.Kf4 and 55...Kg6 56.Ke4 Kf6 57.Kd5 leave White with a winning position. Consider how to preserve the distance before contesting lateral space.
step.t_euwe.hint3: Advancing the pawn or approaching through the center does not settle the race between the two targets: 49.c3 Ke4 50.Kb3 Kd3 and 49.Kd5 a4 50.Kc4 Ke4 lead to drawn positions. Compare the kings’ ranks and the route to a5 before choosing the advance.
step.t_lesson.hint3:
Advancing the pawn early or approaching with the king on the wrong file lets the defender maintain the barrier. Compare the entry square each move prepares.

1.Ke3 Ke7 2.g4 Ke6: allows a draw.

1.g4 Kd7 2.g5 Kd6: allows a draw.
step.t_diagonal.hint3:
Advancing the pawn without support or approaching through the apparently most direct square does not guarantee a key square. The black king can reorganize the opposition.

1.e4 Ke5 2.Ke2 Kxe4: allows a draw.

1.Ke4 Ke6 2.Kd3 Kd5: allows a draw.
step.t_capablanca.hint3:
Stepping sideways before restricting the opposing king allows it to follow. The change of target must be prepared through the contest for opposition.

1.Kd2 Kf7 2.Kc3 Ke6: allows a draw.

1.Kf2 Kd7 2.Ke3 Ke7: allows a draw.
step.t_outflank.hint3:
Switching early to the queenside leaves the black king counterplay against h4. Restrict that access before going around.

1.Kd4 Kf5 2.Kc5 Kg4: allows a draw.

1.Kd5 Kf5 2.Kd4 Kf4: allows a draw.
step.t_edge.hint3:
Approaching without preparing opposition or retreating toward the center lets the black king continue blocking the entry. Compare access to the target after Black’s reply.

1.Kd6 Kb6 2.Ke5 Ka7: allows a draw.

1.Ke4 Ka6 2.Kd3 Ka5: allows a draw.
step.t_edgeCorner.hint3:
An immediate approach lets Black follow along the edge. A waiting move must prepare a relationship between the kings that forces the defender to give way.

1.Ke6 Ka6 2.Ke5 Ka7: allows a draw.

1.Ke7 Ka7 2.Kd6 Kb6: allows a draw.
step.t_waiting.hint3:
Moving the king too early leaves Black a useful pawn advance; spending both pawn advances also allows a draw. Before approaching, compare both sides’ reserves.

1.Kb8 b4 2.cxb4 Kb5: allows a draw.

1.b4 Ka6 2.Kb8 Kb6: allows a draw.
step.t_useReserve.hint3:
Advancing the pawn before capturing the blocker gives time for captures on the other wing. Compare the king’s route with the pawn advance: the two actions have different effects.

1.h6 Kxc4 2.b3+ Kxb3: allows a draw.
step.t_means.hint3:
An unsupported advance lets the opposing king catch and capture the pawn. First organize the squares that make promotion possible.

1.c5 Kd7 2.c6+ Kxc6: allows a draw.
step.t_means.hint2: A key square lets the king support the pawn’s advance even against the best defense. Compare that goal with merely maintaining the confrontation between the kings.
step.d_capablancaReturn: Return to the practice position after 1.Ke2 Kf8 2.Kd3 Ke7. The numbering continues at the third move. The white king should not move up automatically: first regain opposition on the file to which the opponent has returned.
step.d_capablancaReturn.m1: 3.Ke3! The king moves along the rank and leaves three squares between the kings on the e-file, with Black to move. This is the only move that preserves the win. Advancing directly allows a draw: 3.Kd4 Kd6 4.Ke4 Ke6 returns direct opposition to Black; 3.Ke4 Ke6 4.Kd4 Kf5 lets the black king approach h4.
step.d_capablancaReturn.m2: 3...Ke6. The black king reduces the distance. There are now two squares between the kings, and White can respond on the same axis.
step.d_capablancaReturn.m3: 4.Ke4! With the kings on e4 and e6 and Black to move, White takes direct opposition. The position remains winning: the lateral waiting move prepared an effective approach rather than merely adding a step toward the pawns.
